newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HINGIS PREPARES FOR HISTORIC TITLE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS PREPARES FOR HISTORIC TITLE.

text.p: Tennis prodigy Martina Hingis has nothing to lose, except a place in the history books, when she faces French comeback queen Mary Pierce in the Australian Open women's final on Saturday.
The 16-year-old Hingis can become the youngest ever Grand Slam champion by beating Pierce at Melbourne Park and regardless of the outcome will jump to number two in the world rankings.

But the magnitude of the occasion has not overawed the Czechoslovak-born player who was all smiles on Friday after partnering Natasha Zvereva to victory in the women's doubles final to become the youngest Australian Open champion.
Hingis told reporters the 52-minute match doubled as her training session for Saturday's final. "That was practice enough," she said.
After playing perfect tennis to destroy American Mary Joe Fernandez in the semifinals she said she had nothing to lose against Pierce.
But Pierce, who has not dropped a set to her young Swiss rival in their three previous meetings, is counting on Hingis faltering under the pressure from tennis fans anxious to welcome a new darling.

At 16 years, three months and 26 days on the day of the final, Hingis could become the youngest champion at a major since amateur Lottie Dod, aged 15 years and 10 months, won at Wimbledon in 1887 -- before Grand Slams were even invented.
The youngest Grand Slam winner since tennis was opened to professionals in 1968 was Monica Seles, who won the U.S. Open in 1990 aged 16 years and 10 months.
Pierce, who rose to a ranking of three in 1995, feels she is mentally the stronger of the pair and her experience could be the telling factor on Saturday.
"If you haven't been there before you can get a little nervous and then that's where someone who is experienced could realise those things and take advantage of it," said Pierce, the 1995 champion.
Fernandez, who felt the full wrath of a Hingis onslaught on Thursday, feels the young Swiss will be hard pressed to contain her emotions.
"I think she's going to be nervous and the pressure is on her," said the American.
"Mary is going to be confident and she hits hard enough where she can hurt her. I think it's really going to be more up to how Mary plays that decides the outcome of the match."
Hingis has not dropped a set in Melbourne this year but she has a poor record against Pierce. On a black day at the Canadian Open two years ago she failed to even win a game.
Last April on the Hamburg clay, Hingis, then ranked 16 in the world, put up a much stronger fight, losing the first set in a tie-break before fading to lose the second 6-2.
"It's just a different surface and I think I'm a different player since then," said Hingis.
Pierce, who is making a comeback after taking a three-month break from tennis due to injury and stress, believes Hingis has improved since their last meeting.
The 22-year-old, Quebec-born right-hander is enjoying life back on the circuit.
"I've just been having fun, I've just been enjoying it," she said after beating South African Amanda Coetzer in the semifinals.
